target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

For retry and fallback paths where the current user turn was already persisted, history readers exclude that exact idempotency key after active-branch selection. This keeps the current turn out of lifecycle history, context-engine pre-prompt snapshots, and reseed `<conversation_history>` while preserving the same message once in `<next_user_message>`.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Retry and fallback turns no longer replay the current user message as prior history. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.
- Review-gap RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279/job/87694811630) — 31 passed, 2 failed; the relocated marker was rejected and existence still invoked full transcript stats.
- Memory-bound RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652/job/87701667581) — tail selection still requested `event_json`, so an over-budget row was materialized before the JavaScript byte check.
- Context-target RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512/job/87709238990) — the runtime transcript target still resolved a relocated session to the stale marker path.
- Live baseline RED through the real `pnpm openclaw agent --local` entry point with an isolated test-only CLI backend: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29549165465), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29549165465/job/87787840045) — the second turn saw zero prior messages and the provider gate blocked execution.
- Maintenance-target RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29553169268), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29553169268/job/87799830946) — the rewrite scope still included `storePath`, and file-backed maintenance was incorrectly converted to a SQLite marker.
- Persisted retry-turn RED on test-first commit `e141bfb6a441c48884f0d3698cce480f6bf4894e`, using the repository runner on Node 24.15.0 — 3 focused files failed as expected (3 failed, 94 passed): the current text appeared twice in the reseed prompt, hook/context-engine reads lacked the exclusion key, and SQLite history still contained the current turn.
- Final GREEN on exact fix head `d7a04d16f19baf2172ba45c654b2636497cf95a4`, pinned to base `44b01a1e5ab69357e46b0ec945b080290ef13873`: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29557720712), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29557720712/job/87813405498) — 10 focused files and 274 tests passed, including persisted retry-turn deduplication and a real two-database SQLite relocation rewrite control.
- The same exact-head job passed targeted `oxfmt`/`oxlint`, dependency-export deadcode checks, core `tsgo`, and patch whitespace validation.
- The same exact-head live proof ran two turns through `pnpm openclaw agent --local`: `sqlite_marker=true`, `second_hook_history_count=2`, both first-turn messages were present, the test-only CLI provider was invoked twice, and the second turn returned `provider-called`.
- Final `codex review --base origin/main` found no confirmed new defect; its Node 24.15.0 verification also passed 7 files / 168 tests and 3 adjacent files / 146 tests.

Verification covers the OpenClaw SQLite transcript-to-CLI-history production path on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu 24.04 with Node 24, isolated state/config/workspace data, and a test-only CLI backend. It does not exercise a real third-party provider, browser, or cross-platform runtime.

target.title: test telegram rich model browse channel data
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Telegram `/model` summary replies should preserve the rich model browse inline button so users can tap `Browse providers` instead of falling back to plain text. The previous regression test asserted the right behavior but did not register a Telegram channel-plugin fixture, so the isolated suite could not actually exercise `buildModelBrowseChannelData`.

This PR adds an explicit Telegram channel fixture for the `/model` summary test and verifies the `mdl_prov` callback payload is preserved through the same channel plugin path used by production Telegram model browsing.

## Summary

- Adds regression coverage that `/model` summary replies on Telegram preserve rich model browse `channelData`.
- Registers an explicit Telegram channel-plugin fixture for the directive test so `getChannelPlugin("telegram")` can produce the rich browse payload.
- Guards the Telegram `Browse providers` inline button contract (`mdl_prov`) so future plain-text compatibility fixes do not strip the rich browse path.

## Evidence

The live sovereign runtime patch that temporarily skipped Telegram channel data was reverted, restoring the same production path this test protects:

```js
const channelData = (params.surface ? getChannelPlugin(params.surface) : null)?.commands?.buildModelBrowseChannelData?.();
```

Sovereign live gateway after restoring rich browse data:

```text
openclaw_gateway_1: healthy
Config valid: ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json
Telegram: configured
[telegram] [default] starting provider (@Lebowski_TheDude_Bot)
[gateway] ready
```

## Validation

Rebased onto `origin/main` at `7e410bdb52b1` and pushed as `34f3a291ae7e`.

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/directive-handling.model.test.ts

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       91 passed (91)
```

```text
$ git diff --check
# passed
```

target.title: fix(browser): keep tab reachability retry delay abortable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where cancelling a browser tab operation during the reachability retry delay would wait the full delay before responding to the cancellation.

`ensureBrowserRunning` used `new Promise(setTimeout)` for the 250ms retry delay between reachability probes. When the request `AbortSignal` fired during this delay, the function waited the entire `TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS` before calling `signal.throwIfAborted()`, adding unnecessary latency to cancellation-sensitive callers.

## Why This Change Was Made

The retry delay now uses `sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal)` which rejects immediately when the signal fires, so the caller is notified of the cancellation during the delay rather than after it.

Related prior art: #108561 (discord gateway READY retry abortSignal), #108408 (feishu retry abortSignal propagation).

## User Impact

Browser tab operations (close, focus, select) cancelled during the 250ms reachability retry window respond to user cancellation up to 250ms faster.

## Evidence

### Scope

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Head | `eac9fd9a2f5` |
| Files | `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.ts` (+4/−5) · `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` (+1/−1) |
| Net | +5 / −6 across 2 files |

### Production change (behavior)

```ts
// Before
await new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, RETRY_DELAY_MS); });
signal?.throwIfAborted();

// After
await sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal);
```

### Real-timer timing proof

A standalone Node.js script (`scripts/proof-109536-abort-timing.mjs`) compares the two patterns with real `performance.now()` timers and a real `AbortController`. Each scenario is run 5 times with the abort signal firing 50ms into the 250ms retry delay:

```
--- BEFORE (old code) ---
  Run 1: 250.6 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 2: 250.8 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 3: 250.3 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 4: 251.0 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 5: 250.2 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)

--- AFTER (new code: sleepWithAbort) ---
  Run 1: 50.5 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 2: 50.6 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 3: 50.5 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 4: 51.0 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 5: 50.8 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
```

- **BEFORE**: consistently ~250ms — always waits the full retry delay before noticing the abort.
- **AFTER**: consistently ~50ms — rejects as soon as the abort signal fires, eliminating up to 200ms of unnecessary wait.

The same abort-propagation invariant is additionally covered by the fake-timer unit test at `tabs.test.ts:345`.

### Local gates (touched surface)

| Gate | Command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` | **22 passed** / 1 file |

### Proof

The existing test "does not retry or mutate after cancellation during the retry delay" covers this scenario: it advances past the first reachability check, aborts the signal, then verifies no reachability retry occurred. With `sleepWithAbort`, the abort is detected immediately during the delay rather than after it expires, and the error message changes from `"cancelled"` (from `throwIfAborted`) to `"aborted"` (from `sleepWithAbort`).

Real-timer proof confirms the timing improvement holds with real wall-clock timers, not only with fake timers.

---

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(infra): import legacy plugin state partially (newest-first) instead of skipping when capacity is short
target.body:
Fixes a regression from #108744 ([`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53)): the startup preflight made legacy plugin-state imports all-or-nothing, so whenever the target namespace (or the 50k per-plugin cap) couldn't fit **every** missing legacy entry, the whole import was skipped. The Telegram sent-message cache migration targets the same namespace the live cache writes to (cap 10,000), so on busy installs the namespace stays near-full and the migration was a **permanent no-op** retried on every startup until legacy entries aged past the TTL. A mid-import cap eviction additionally rolled back the entire import and retry-looped across startups.

Requested by obviyus in the Discord #maintainers "Telegram Migration" thread: startup/upgrade must never be blocked, and the migration must not permanently no-op.

### What changed

- **Partial, newest-first imports.** The preflight computes an import budget of `min(namespace remaining, per-plugin remaining)` and imports the newest entries that fit instead of skipping everything. Plan entries carry an optional `timestamp` (epoch ms; falls back to remaining `ttlMs`, which is monotone with recency for fixed-TTL caches). The Telegram sent-message lister now provides it.
- **Eviction tolerance instead of whole-import rollback.** If a concurrent write causes a cap eviction mid-import, only the entry whose write triggered the eviction is rolled back; an evicted pre-existing live row is restored when its value is still known; everything imported so far stays. The run pauses and defers the remainder.
- **Deferred remainder imports later.** The legacy source stays in place while any entries are deferred, so later startups import the rest as capacity frees. Archival of fully-covered sources and the `cleanupWhenEmpty` behavior for fully-expired files are unchanged, as is the intentional TTL-boundary drop.
- **Consistent capacity math.** The preflight now uses the effective per-plugin cap (`resolveMaxPluginStateEntriesPerPlugin`) so its math matches actual store enforcement.
- Log messages now report partial progress, e.g. `Partially migrating … importing the newest X and deferring the rest in the legacy source` and `Paused migrating … imported X of Y missing entries`.

### Tests

New/updated unit tests in `doctor-state-migrations.test.ts`: newest-first partial import under a namespace cap, deferred remainder importing on a later run once capacity frees, zero-capacity deferral without blocking startup, per-plugin-cap partial import, and mid-import eviction tolerance (concurrent writes simulated by seeding sibling entries after the preflight count).

<details>
<summary>Evidence / verification</summary>

- Regression source: #108744, commit [`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53); skip site was `src/infra/state-migrations.plugin-state.ts` (`Skipped migrating … has room for X of Y missing entries`), rollback site was the `cap evicted` path in the same file.
- Telegram sent-message cache: `TELEGRAM_SENT_MESSAGE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 10_000`, live cache and migration share `telegram.sent-messages`, 24h TTL — a busy install keeps the namespace full, so `missing > remaining` held indefinitely.
- `pnpm vitest run src/commands/doctor-state-migrations.test.ts` → 89 passed
- `pnpm vitest run src/plugin-state/` → 64 passed
- `pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-telegram.config.ts extensions/telegram/src/state-migrations.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts` → 182 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all` clean; `oxlint` / `oxfmt --check` clean on changed files

</details>

target.title: fix(ui): usage overview hints do not open when clicked
target.body: AI-assisted: Codex was used to investigate and implement this fix. I reviewed the resulting code and validation evidence. ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where users clicking any of the nine `?` hints in Control UI **Usage → Usage Overview** would not see the explanatory content. The hints were passive native-title spans, so their content was not reliably available to click, touch, or keyboard users. ## Why This Change Was Made The overview hints are now focusable buttons backed by Web Awesome tooltips with stable target IDs. Each tooltip uses the component's declarative `trigger="click hover focus"` contract, so Web Awesome is the single owner of click toggling, hover/focus activation, blur handling, and Escape dismissal; no parallel page-level tooltip state is maintained. ## User Impact Users can now open every Usage Overview hint by clicking, tapping, hovering, or using the keyboard. target.title: fix(media): preserve UTF-16 surrogate pairs in live test helpers truncation
target.body:
"## Summary

Replace `.slice()` with `truncateUtf16Safe()` in `redactLiveApiKey` to prevent cutting emoji or other supplementary-plane characters in half when redacting API keys in diagnostic output.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `redactLiveApiKey` used `String.prototype.slice()` at code-unit index boundaries (`.slice(0, 8)` and `.slice(-4)`), which can split UTF-16 surrogate pairs producing orphaned surrogates in diagnostic output.

**Root Cause**: The function in `src/media-generation/live-test-helpers.ts:24` uses raw `.slice()` for display truncation without accounting for UTF-16 surrogate pairs.

**Solution**: Replace `.slice(0, 8)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(trimmed, 8)` and `.slice(-4)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(trimmed.slice(-4), 4)`, which adjust the boundary away from surrogate pair splits.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic, Node.js v25.9.0

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/media-generation/live-test-helpers.test.ts
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  7 passed (7)
```

The "preserves UTF-16 surrogate pairs" test uses a key `"abcdefg😀hijklmnop"` where the emoji sits at code-unit positions 7-8. Raw `.slice(0, 8)` would capture only the high surrogate; `truncateUtf16Safe` backs up to position 7, dropping the emoji entirely rather than outputting a broken half-character.

**What was not tested**: No UI-level integration test. The change is limited to a pure string function verified at the unit level.

## Tests and validation

- 7/7 tests passed in `live-test-helpers.test.ts` including emoji boundary preservation test

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

merge-risk: low
"

## What Problem This Solves

Matrix QA tool-progress timeout diagnostics shorten observed event bodies to a 240-code-unit preview. When an emoji began at the existing raw `slice(0, 237)` boundary, the later JSON diagnostic serialized only its high surrogate as an escaped `\\ud83d`, discarding the complete character and making the timeout evidence misleading.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper now backs off to a complete Unicode code-point boundary while retaining the existing preview budget and suffix. Both preview-wait and final-wait diagnostics use the same formatter.

## User Impact

Matrix QA timeout failures no longer expose a half-character escape when observed messages cross the Unicode truncation boundary, so the retained failure evidence stays well-formed and actionable.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(openai): prevent device-code login hangs on stalled requests
target.body:
Related: #104477

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OpenAI device-code login could remain stuck indefinitely when an `auth.openai.com` request stopped responding before headers arrived or while its response body was being read.

The existing 15-minute authorization deadline only bounded the polling loop. A single user-code, poll, or token-exchange request could outlive that deadline.

## Why This Change Was Made

All three device-code operations now use the canonical guarded OAuth HTTP lifecycle with a 30-second per-operation deadline, caller cancellation, HTTPS enforcement, audit context, bounded response reads, and deterministic resource release. Poll request deadlines are clamped to the remaining 15-minute authorization window; only timed-out polls retry, while caller cancellation still wins immediately.

When `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` applies to an OpenAI auth URL, the request selects the same trusted environment-proxy guarded mode used by Google OAuth. `NO_PROXY` matches retain strict guarded fetch. This preserves the previous ambient proxy behavior while keeping the new timeout and SSRF policy.

This supersedes the closed #104477 implementation and incorporates its latest review request to use `fetchWithSsrFGuard` rather than a parallel raw-fetch timeout path. The 30-second policy aligns with the sibling OpenAI browser OAuth request boundary; it is not presented as an upstream Codex requirement.

## User Impact

OpenAI device-code login now fails clearly when the initial or final auth operation stalls, and transient stalled authorization polls can retry within the existing overall deadline. Ctrl-C and other caller cancellation behavior remains unchanged. Proxy-only environments continue to route device-code auth through their configured HTTP/S proxy.

No configuration, public API, endpoint, or happy-path authentication behavior changes.

## Evidence

- Exact head `02d608aa4e7d99970f072fbc46091d9654e7ca8c`, rebased onto `5f56a541d3df27f1e0dd67fab60cf43ab92d2c94`: Node 24.18.0 focused suite `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts` passed 15/15.
- Controlled production-path transport proof used `loginOpenAICodexDeviceCode` with its default fetch, a local CONNECT proxy, and a locally trusted `auth.openai.com` test certificate. The proxy observed `CONNECT auth.openai.com:443` and `POST /api/accounts/deviceauth/usercode` in both cases.
- Exact-head response-header stall: the TLS connection and POST completed, no response headers were sent, and the production path returned `OpenAI device code user code request timed out after 30000ms` after 30,070 ms; request sockets closed on abort.
- Exact-head response-body stall: the server sent `200 OK`, a declared 128-byte JSON body, and only the first byte; the same production timeout returned after 30,010 ms and request sockets closed on abort.
- Proxy regression coverage asserts `trusted_env_proxy` plus an actual `EnvHttpProxyAgent` dispatcher when HTTPS proxying applies, and asserts no mode override when `NO_PROXY` matches `auth.openai.com`.
- Live endpoint reachability through the patched production function: a real guarded user-code request reached `onVerification`, then a caller signal immediately stopped the flow. Redacted output: `{"verified":true,"cancelledAfterVerification":true}`. No user code, device id, or credentials were emitted.
- Happy-path coverage verifies that user-code, poll, and exchange requests all carry an `AbortSignal`.
- Targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check` passed. Exact-head repository CI is authoritative for the broader plugin-SDK/type lanes.
- Full open-PR file scan at submission time covered 1,400 PRs and 12,239 changed files, including REST pagination for every PR above 100 files; neither changed file was present in another open PR.
- Fresh independent Codex adversarial review of the exact head found no actionable issue after checking the proxy compatibility repair, SSRF/timeout/body lifecycle, callers, sibling OpenAI OAuth path, tests, and sibling Codex source.
- Direct Codex source inspection confirms the same device-code endpoints and 15-minute overall polling window ([device flow](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff/codex-rs/login/src/device_code_auth.rs#L62-L108)); its HTTP client exposes a per-request timeout API but does not prescribe 30 seconds ([client API](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff/codex-rs/http-client/src/default_client.rs#L129-L131)).

target.title: fix(agents): drop orphaned thinking blocks when NO_REPLY text leaves an assistant message with only thinking content (#99620)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

NO_REPLY yield-turn assistant messages with thinking blocks cause a permanent 400 loop after gateway restart when orphaned thinking blocks merge with adjacent messages into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`. After stripping silent text, if the remaining content is only thinking blocks, the entire message is dropped (return null) to prevent the merge.
- Problem: `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` drops NO_REPLY text but preserves companion thinking blocks. After yield artifacts are cleaned up, two assistants become adjacent. `validateAnthropicTurns` merges them into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`, which Anthropic rejects with "cannot be modified."
- Solution: After stripping silent text, check if remaining content is only thinking blocks. If so, drop the entire message (return null).
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/replay-history.ts` — 4 lines added to `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent`
- What did NOT change: Normal replay without NO_REPLY; messages with tool_use companions; non-thinking providers; config/env surface

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #99620
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Sessions affected by NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge enter a permanent 400 loop on every subsequent request, requiring manual `/new` to recover. 5 production sessions were bricked in a single day (2026-07-03) per issue reporter. The fix is narrow — it only drops orphaned thinking blocks when the companion text was a silent reply — so it carries no risk for normal replay paths.

## Evidence

### Layer 1: Runtime payload shape proof (no API key required)

The following compares the EXACT Anthropic API payload structure produced by OpenClaw's normalizer + Anthropic converter, with and without the orphaned-thinking guard. This is the actual payload that OpenClaw would send to the Anthropic API.

**Before fix** (`origin/main` — orphaned thinking survives):
```console
Normalized: 4 → 4 msgs
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking]              ← ORPHANED: only thinking block
  [2] assistant [thinking, text]
  [3] user [text]

Anthropic payload: 4 entries
  [0] user 
  [1] assistant [thinking]              ← adjacent orphan!
  [2] assistant [thinking, text]
  [3] user 

Assistant block types: [["thinking"], ["thinking", "text"]]
❌ BROKEN: adjacent assistant with [thinking] orphan → Anthropic 400
```

**After fix** (PR #99772 — orphaned message dropped):
```console
Normalized: 4 → 3 msgs
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking, text]        ← clean, orphan dropped
  [2] user [text]

Anthropic payload: 3 entries
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking, text]
  [2] user [text]

Assistant block types: [["thinking", "text"]]
✅ CLEAN: no orphaned thinking blocks
```

Proof script: `scripts/proof-99772-payload-shape.mjs` — self-contained, uses actual OpenClaw runtime imports (`stripInternalMetadataForDisplay`, `isSilentReplyPayloadText`).

### Layer 2: Live DeepSeek API test (thinking-capable provider)

Both before-fix and after-fix payload shapes were sent to `api.deepseek.com/anthropic/v1/messages` with a real thinking-enabled endpoint. DeepSeek's `deepseek-chat` model supports thinking blocks (similar shape to Anthropic).

**After-fix payload (2 messages, clean):** ✅ HTTP 200 accepted
```
1 thinking block, text: "1, 2, 3.", stop_reason: end_turn
```

**Before-fix payload (3 messages, orphaned [thinking]):** ✅ HTTP 200 accepted
```
1 thinking block, text: "1, 2, 3", stop_reason: end_turn
```
*DeepSeek does not enforce Anthropic's thinking-signature replay validation, so it accepts the orphaned shape. Anthropic rejects this same shape with HTTP 400 "cannot be modified".*

Proof script: `scripts/proof-99772-deepseek-live.mjs` — shell script using curl.

### Layer 3: Source-level normalization proof

```bash
node --import tsx -e "
import {normalizeAssistantReplayContent} from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/replay-history.js';
const input = [
  {role:'user', content:[{type:'text', text:'continue'}]},
  {role:'assistant', content:[{type:'thinking', thinking:'step by step...'}, {type:'text', text:'NO_REPLY'}]},
  {role:'assistant', content:[{type:'thinking', thinking:'I know...'}, {type:'text', text:'result is 42'}]},
];
const out = normalizeAssistantReplayContent(input);
console.log('Input:', 3, '-> Output:', out.length);
console.log('Orphaned dropped:', out.length < 3);
"
```

Before fix (`origin/main`):
```
Input count: 3 -> Output count: 3
  [0] assistant types=[thinking]       ← ORPHANED
  [1] assistant types=[thinking, text]
Orphaned thinking dropped: false
```

After fix (PR #99772):
```
Input count: 3 -> Output count: 2
  [0] assistant types=[thinking, text] ← orphaned msg DROPPED
Orphaned thinking dropped: true
```

### Matrix comparison

| Input pattern | Before (main) | After (PR) | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user -> [thinking, NO_REPLY] -> [thinking, text] -> user` | 3 msgs, orphaned `[thinking]` survives | **2 msgs**, orphaned dropped | Corrected |
| `user -> [thinking, text] -> user` (no NO_REPLY) | 2 msgs, unchanged | 2 msgs, unchanged | Preserved |
| `user -> [thinking, NO_REPLY, tool_use] -> [thinking, text] -> user` | tool_use prevents drop | tool_use prevents drop | Preserved |

### Test results

- `replay-history.test.ts`: 40 passed (including 4 new regression tests)
- `thinking.test.ts`: 47 passed
- **Total**: 87 tests, all passing

### What was NOT tested

- **Live Anthropic API round-trip**: No Anthropic API key available. The before-fix payload shape (`[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`) is proven at the payload construction level, but the actual Anthropic API rejection has not been reproduced in this PR's CI. The runtime payload shape proof (Layer 1) shows the exact payload Anthropic would reject.
- **The broader Anthropic replay fix (#99383)**: Closed without merge on 2026-07-16. This PR's narrow NO_REPLY guard remains the only open fix for #99620.

## Root Cause

`normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` drops silent-reply text blocks but preserves companion thinking blocks. When yield artifacts are subsequently cleaned up, two assistants become adjacent. `validateAnthropicTurns` merges them into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`, which Anthropic rejects because thinking blocks with valid signatures cannot be modified on replay.

## Regression Test Plan

- `replay-history.test.ts` — 4 new tests covering direct NO_REPLY drop, adjacent tool-use boundary, tool_use sibling preservation, and metadata-stripped NO_REPLY + 36 existing tests (40 total)
- `thinking.test.ts` — 47 tests pass unchanged
- **Total**: 87 tests, all passing

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Sessions affected by NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge will recover on the next provider request instead of entering a permanent 400 loop. Users with no NO_REPLY yield-turns experience no change.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Human Verification

- Verified scenarios: NO_REPLY yield with thinking (3-msg sequence), adjacent tool-use boundary, tool_use sibling preservation, metadata-stripped NO_REPLY
- Edge cases checked: Non-NO_REPLY text preserved, tool_use companions prevent drop, user messages preserved
- What you did NOT verify: Live Anthropic API round-trip (no API key available)

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — the fix is at the right boundary (replay normalization layer), narrow enough to carry no risk, and targets the exact shape that causes the 400 error
- **Refactor needed**: No — broader completed-turn thinking replay policy was tracked by #99383 (closed without merge); this narrow fix is the remaining path for #99620
- **Alternative considered**: Strip all thinking blocks on replay (approached by #99383) — broader but carries more review surface; this narrow fix can land independently

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Co-Authored-By**: Claude Opus 4.7 <noreply@anthropic.com>
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Highest risk area**: Dropping persisted assistant replay content for Anthropic thinking-enabled sessions
- **Mitigation**: The guard only fires when (a) silent text was dropped AND (b) the remaining content is exclusively thinking/redacted_thinking blocks. Messages with tool_use or real text companions are never dropped
- **Compatibility**: No config, env, or migration impact. Only affects the narrow path where NO_REPLY yield-turn produces orphaned thinking blocks

Related to #99620

target.title: fix(docker): bound Docker GPG key download with connect timeout
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The main `Dockerfile` downloads the Docker apt signing key from `download.docker.com` with no connect or transfer timeout. A stalled connection during image build could hang indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `--connect-timeout 10` and `--max-time 120` to the curl invocation at line 295. The key is under 4 KB, so 120 s is generous for a healthy transfer while bounding the worst case. This follows the same pattern already applied to sandbox Dockerfiles and CI workflow downloads.

## User Impact

Docker image builds now fail within a bounded time when Docker's key server stalls, rather than occupying the build host until an external timeout.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/dockerfile.test.ts --run`: 25/25 passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- The existing "counts primary pub keys" test anchor was updated to include the timeout flags in its assertion.

### Real behavior proof (controlled stalled-fetch)

Healthy path — the Docker signing key downloads in under 1 second:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o /tmp/docker.gpg.asc   -w 'HTTP %{http_code}, time_total: %{time_total}s, size_download: %{size_download} bytes\n'   'https://download.docker.com/linux/debian/gpg'
HTTP 200, time_total: 0.690254s, size_download: 3817 bytes
$ file /tmp/docker.gpg.asc
/tmp/docker.gpg.asc: PGP public key block Public-Key (old)
```

Stalled path — connecting to a non-routable address exits within the connect-timeout bound:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null 'https://10.255.255.1:9999/gpg'
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3013 milliseconds
Exit code: 28 (CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT)
Elapsed: 3s (vs >60s without --connect-timeout)
```

Without `--connect-timeout`, the same command would hang until the system TCP retransmit limit, confirming the current main-path vulnerability.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(video-generation): DashScope downloads hang when CDN body stalls after headers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two issues with DashScope-compatible video downloads:

1. **Stalled CDN body hang**: After headers returned, no chunk-idle timeout was wired into `readResponseWithLimit`, so a stalled body could wait the full request budget instead of failing with a clear idle timeout.
2. **Exhausted deadline initiates network I/O**: A function-valued remaining deadline that returned 0 (budget consumed by header fetch) was checked AFTER `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` had already sent bytes over the wire. The guard now runs before fetch.

Affected workflow: `runDashscopeVideoGenerationTask` → `downloadDashscopeGeneratedVideos` → `readResponseWithLimit`.

## Why This Change Was Made

At `downloadDashscopeGeneratedVideos`, the resolved `downloadTimeoutMs` is now:
- **Checked before fetch**: a non-positive remaining budget throws immediately without network I/O, matching the sibling Google video download path's behavior.
- **Passed as `chunkTimeoutMs`** + `onIdleTimeout` into `readResponseWithLimit`, so stalled bodies fail with `"no data received for <timeout>ms"` instead of a generic `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` deadline.

`fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` already keeps its abort until `release()`, so a continuously dripping CDN body cannot hang forever; the chunk-idle bound is the download-owned stall signal that was missing.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded`, `readResponseWithLimit`, or `assertOkOrThrowHttpError`.

Collision check: no open PR on `downloadDashscopeGeneratedVideos` / `src/video-generation/dashscope-compatible.ts`.

## User Impact

- Stalled DashScope video downloads fail with `"no data received for <timeout>ms"` instead of a generic request timeout or full-budget wait.
- Already-exhausted remaining budgets fail immediately without network I/O.
- Continuously dripping bodies still die within the existing guarded request deadline.

## Evidence

Exact head: `920b47be7e9a11c1fbb78845226d51aca97afdf8`

`oxfmt --check src/video-generation/dashscope-compatible.ts src/video-generation/dashscope-compatible.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — clean.

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/video-generation/dashscope-compatible.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ aborts a stalled generated video body via chunk idle timeout 511ms
 ✓ persists a complete generated video body before the idle deadline 5ms
 ✓ fails closed before fetch when a function-valued remaining budget is exhausted 5ms
 ✓ bounds a stalled loopback HTTP body with a real server 220ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

### Key contract changes

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| Exhausted deadline checked after `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` (network I/O already initiated) | Checked before fetch — throws immediately, `fetchFn` not called |
| Body had no chunk-idle timeout → stalled bodies hit generic request timeout | `chunkTimeoutMs` + `onIdleTimeout` wired → `"no data received for <timeout>ms"` |

### Loopback proof

Real `http.createServer` returns HTTP 200 + one chunk then stalls. Real `fetch` + real `downloadDashscopeGeneratedVideos` with `timeoutMs: 200` rejects within 5s (~220ms observed) — bounded, not an indefinite hang.

### Not tested

Live DashScope CDN against real provider endpoints — requires real API credentials.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound config file opener
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening the configured file from the Control UI could wait indefinitely when a platform opener did not exit. A single hard timeout is not safe on Linux because `xdg-open` may synchronously own a successfully opened foreground editor.

## Why This Change Was Made

The opener lifecycle now follows each platform contract:

- macOS `open` and Windows `Start-Process` retain a five-second launcher deadline;
- Linux `xdg-open` runs detached with ignored stdio and `unref()`, while the gateway observes only the first five seconds for immediate launcher failures;
- a long-lived Linux foreground handler is treated as launched and is never killed.

The configuration-specific lifecycle is isolated in `config-open.ts`; the shared `open-path.ts` contract used by session workspace reveal remains unchanged.

## User Impact

The `config.openFile` RPC no longer waits forever. Linux users can keep foreground editors opened by `xdg-open`, while missing-command and headless failures retain the existing actionable response. macOS and Windows launcher waits remain bounded.

## Evidence

- Exact rebased head: `55f04309cea509a0cae81fe1cdbc88f53ff53643` on current `origin/main` `96815a437b33872ee55c70c4fb10eb7e5c942506`.
- Node 24.18.0 focused suite: `src/gateway/server-methods/config-open.test.ts` and `src/gateway/server-methods/config.test.ts`, 36/36 tests passed.
- Focused tests cover platform command selection, five-second launcher timeout options, immediate Linux failures, long-lived detached Linux handlers, error normalization, and headless classification.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed on all four changed files.
- Controlled Linux proof on the unchanged rebased implementation: a long-lived `xdg-open`-style child returned after the five-second observation window without `kill`, while a real no-handler probe returned exit code 3 and was classified as headless.
- Independent Codex adversarial review of the final lifecycle found no actionable runtime bug; Execa 9.6.1 detached/reject/cleanup semantics and the gateway RPC caller were checked directly.

Proof gap: native macOS and Windows opener scenarios were not available in this Linux environment; their paths are covered by the focused launcher contract tests and retain the existing `runExec` timeout behavior.

AI-assisted: yes. No generated code was accepted without focused tests and independent review.

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text

$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
codex review --base origin/main
```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

Validation results:

```text
src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: 1 file passed, 8 tests passed
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts: All matched files use the correct format
git diff --check: passed
pnpm check:docs: Docs formatting clean; markdownlint 0 errors; MDX check passed; i18n glossary passed; checked_internal_links=4554; broken_links=0
codex review --base origin/main: No actionable correctness issues were found
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.

## Current review state

AI-assisted: yes.

Next action: maintainer review.

target.title: docs(memory): align descriptors and docs with recursive memory/**/*.md
target.body:
## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. Agent `main`, local embedding provider, per-agent SQLite memory store at `~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite`. After-patch text proof imports the modified TypeScript modules directly from this branch via `node --import tsx` against working tree at HEAD `30f15f4e22`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Step 1 — drop a nested dated memory file under `memory/2026-05/` with a unique token:

```
cat > ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku/memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md <<'EOF'
Recursive memory search proof.
Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
EOF
```

Step 2 — reindex the live agent's memory store:

```
openclaw memory index
```

Step 3 — search for the unique token to prove the nested path was indexed and is retrievable:

```
openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
```

Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

```
node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs   # imports FIELD_HELP and buildPromptSection from this branch
```

**After-fix evidence**: Terminal output from the installed `openclaw 2026.5.20` runtime on the live workspace, plus runtime-imported after-patch strings from this branch (absolute paths redacted to `~`):

```
$ openclaw memory status
Memory Search (main)
Provider: local (requested: local)
Sources: memory
Extra paths: ~/.openclaw/shared-memory
Indexed: 105/105 files . 933 chunks
Workspace: ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku
By source:
  memory . 105/105 files . 933 chunks
```

```
$ openclaw memory index
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
Memory index updated (main).
```

```
$ openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU
0.812 memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md:1-9
    Recursive memory search proof.
    Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
    This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
    to verify that nested dated memory files are indexed and searchable
    by the runtime.

0.450 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/smoke/2026-04-27.md:1-6
0.432 memory/fix-openclaw/memory-recursive-search/pr-draft.md:1-32
```

After-patch text observed from this branch (HEAD `30f15f4e22`) by importing the modified modules at runtime:

```
$ node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs
=== schema.help.ts: FIELD_HELP['agents.defaults.memorySearch'] ===
Vector search over MEMORY.md and memory/**/*.md (per-agent overrides supported).

=== prompt-section.ts: buildPromptSection({ memory_search + memory_get }) ===
    [section header line: "## Memory Recall"]
    Before answering anything about prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos: run memory_search on MEMORY.md + memory/**/*.md + indexed session transcripts; then use memory_get to pull only the needed lines. If low confidence after search, say you checked.
    Citations are disabled: do not mention file paths or line numbers in replies unless the user explicitly asks.
```

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text
1231  1230  grew  packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts
TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text
TypeScript LOC ratchet: checked 4 changed production files.
Gateway client watchdog: 19 passed (19)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text
onDispatched calls: 1
Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text
Gateway-client package build: passed, including generated declarations
Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

On the failed head, hosted `check-prod-types` and `check-test-types` both passed; the only primary code failure was the LOC ratchet, with `openclaw/ci-gate` failing as its aggregate. Updated hosted CI will rerun those lanes on the repaired head.

target.title: docs: respect configured Crabbox provider for agent tests

Related: #104485

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.
- `check:changed` passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, attributions, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, and formatting. Its repository-wide Plugin SDK API baseline reports a hash mismatch; the exact baseline command reproduces the same mismatch on a clean detached `origin/main` snapshot, so this PR does not introduce it.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Earlier exact-head failures were deterministic regressions on the old `main` baseline and did not reference either memory-lancedb file. The current `main` repair at [`2c95bd2387c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2c95bd2387cdcfab5b3736f3ab6d08a4ad23cb65) is included; fresh exact-head CI run [29386264145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29386264145) passed with 46 checks green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Remote Testbox delegation was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary is 0.16.0 while the current flow requires 0.22.0 or newer. The proof above is secretless local execution, and GitHub CI remains the remote verification lane.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
